title: Operator precedence, associativity and expression grouping
learningObjectives: Explain how operator precedence determines grouping in an expression.
Explain how associativity groups operators of the same precedence.
Use parentheses to make intended evaluation explicit.
Distinguish expression grouping from the order in which operands are evaluated.
Avoid relying on unspecified or unsequenced side-effect order.

understand.concept: Operator precedence and associativity determine how tokens in an expression are grouped by the C grammar. They do not, by themselves, specify the order in which operands are evaluated. Parentheses can clarify or change grouping, but they do not automatically impose an evaluation order on every subexpression. Expressions with unsequenced conflicting side effects can have undefined behavior.
understand.whyItMatters: Understanding Operator precedence, associativity and expression grouping helps you reason about program behaviour instead of memorizing syntax. It is useful in exams, debugging and building reliable C applications.
understand.analogy: Treat the concept as a tool with a precise contract: it has valid inputs, defined operations and observable results.
understand.analogyLimit: An analogy is only an aid; the C standard and the relevant function specifications determine actual behaviour.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Precedence

Precedence determines which operators bind more tightly. For example, multiplication has higher precedence than addition, so `2 + 3 * 4` groups as `2 + (3 * 4)`.

## 2. Associativity

When operators of the same precedence appear together, associativity determines grouping. Most arithmetic binary operators group left to right, while assignment operators group right to left. This is a grammar rule, not a promise about execution order of every operand.

## 3. Parentheses communicate intent

Write `(a + b) * c` when the addition must be grouped before multiplication. Parentheses reduce ambiguity for readers and prevent mistakes when the default precedence is not obvious.

## 4. Grouping is not evaluation order

The expression `f() + g()` does not generally specify whether f or g is called first. Do not confuse precedence with sequencing. Avoid expressions that modify the same scalar object in unsequenced ways, because they can have undefined behavior.

## 5. Prefer clear expressions

Break complicated calculations into named intermediate variables. Use parentheses when they make the intended grouping visible, and consult a precedence table when needed.
